projects.title: AI Clinical Care Knowledge Tool
projects.description:
Included Health has the unique challenge of having millions of members to cater to across a number of offerings including direct line of site care (primary care), longitudinal health, healthcare navigation, billing support, and many others. The volume of calls and documents (which oftentimes includes a patients' full, unedited medical record) can be overwhelming. This is why the KS (Knowledge System) was developed. So that when a patient calls in, the right answers are at the fingertips of the Customer Care Advocate immediately.

I designed the system to make full use of LLMs and RAG, simultaneously searching millions of documents — both care-related and patient-specific — to surface the right answer in context. 

The results were measurable: the system reduced AHT (Average Handle Time) by an average of 1.5 minutes per case, a meaningful cost savings at scale, without compromising the quality of care Included Health is known for.

projects.title: AI Healthcare Companion
projects.description:
Founded in 2023, Noodle started as a RAG-based note-taking app and evolved into something more ambitious: a platform designed to give patients real ownership of their health information. The focus shifted to people managing complex, multi-specialist conditions — the kind that generate scattered records, forgotten instructions, and fragmented data across providers.

The core insight was that health record balkanization is the root problem. Noodle addresses it by letting people capture and consolidate health events through whatever channel is easiest — web app, WhatsApp, voice, or images — and then surfaces that information through a conversational UI, making it genuinely useful rather than just stored.

Working with my co-founder, Julz Bautista, we raised an angel round and generated significant interest from partners and members of the healthcare community. The platform leverages LLMs, vector search (RAG), personal health journaling, health record consolidation, and self-sampling to help surface actionable insights and enable more meaningful interactions between patients and their physicians. 

Noodle is closed to new sign ups but still servicing a number of patients who entrusted their information to the service.
projects.involvement:
I co-founded Noodle and led the end-to-end design and co-lead engineering. I designed the app and co-built the platform using Next.js (TypeScript), Tailwind, and Supabase/Postgres with PGVector for RAG, along wtih contract engineers. 

For AI, we integrated multiple LLM engines — OpenAI, Hugging Face (Meditron-7B/Mistral), and Claude — depending on the task. Added Twilio for WhatsApp-based capture, Deepgram for voice transcription, and RapidAPI for image tagging, OCR, and recognition. The multimodal voice experience was built in Swift.

projects.title: GenSynth ML Explainability Tool
projects.description:
DarwinAI’s GenSynth platform was built to address the deep learning “black box” problem by making convolutional neural networks more transparent and more efficient. For this project, I designed an interface that helped ML practitioners define confusion matrices, inspect misclassified samples, and trace how CNNs learned from training images, with a particular focus on self-driving vehicle perception workflows.

The experience surfaced neuron- and layer-level signals that made it easier to understand which features were driving specific decisions, identify bias and edge cases, and refine models through iteration rather than treating them as opaque systems. The result was a more usable environment for exploring experiments, comparing model variants, and moving toward compact, high-performing networks suitable for real-time edge deployment in safety-critical contexts.
projects.involvement: Principal Designer. I led UX research, interaction design, prototyping, and visual design for the project, mapping the ML workflow and shaping the core explainability and performance-analysis experience in close collaboration with the DarwinAI team.

projects.title: Multimodal AI Transformation
projects.description:
At Included Health, I designed and prototyped a number of AI-based experiences to explore how natural language interfaces could streamline patient intake, streamline physician workflow, reduce documentation time, and improve accessibility. The goal was to evaluate whether a conversational experience could make healthcare interactions more human, intuitive, and efficient — especially in high-friction, high-stakes environments like telehealth and care navigation.

I led the end-to-end experience design, from conversation flow mapping and prompt engineering to interface prototyping and voice synthesis integration. The prototype supported real-time, conversational data capture and retrieval, enabling users to speak naturally and receive intelligent, context-aware responses from the assistant.

To bring the prototype to life, I used Cursor and v0 to build the interface, and integrated OpenAI's language models for NLU and ElevenLabs for synthetic voice output, creating a lifelike interaction loop. I collaborated with clinical ops and engineering stakeholders to align the voice experience with real-world care workflows and regulatory considerations.

The project was always dual-purpose: redesign a broken flow, and learn something meaningful about patient preferences for AI in healthcare. We ran a structured Maze experiment to test all three experiences (original UI, chat-based LLM, and voice-based LLM) head-to-head, and voice came out ahead by a wider margin than anyone anticipated — a finding that shifted how the team thought about conversational AI across the board.

The research directly informed the design language and interaction patterns for AI experiences across several subsequent projects at Included Health, establishing a foundation for how the team approached conversational UI going forward.
projects.involvement: As the lead on this initiative, I was responsible for the full prototype lifecycle — from conversation flow design and prompt engineering to TypeScript/Vercel implementation with OpenAI and ElevenLabs. I collaborated directly with clinical, product, and leadership stakeholders to validate and ship the experience, and championed AI-assisted design workflows across the team, introducing tools like v0, Cursor, Lovable, and GitHub Copilot.

projects.title: Google Mobile Search & Apps
projects.description:
At Google, I led design on the Mobile Search team during one of the most significant platform shifts in the company's history — the move from desktop to touch-based mobile interfaces. My work centered on reimagining how billions of people access information on the go, with a particular focus on local discovery, contextual search, and the emerging behaviors of smartphone users.

The challenge was genuinely hard: search on a 3.5-inch touchscreen isn't just a smaller version of desktop search — it's a fundamentally different problem. Users are on the move, time-pressured, often using imprecise input methods. I designed interaction patterns, result layouts, and suggestion systems that adapted to context — a user's location, time of day, query intent — to surface the most relevant information at the right moment.

I was among the first designers at Google working on touch-native iPhone experiences, and the work had real scale — features I designed shipped to millions of users globally. The team operated at the intersection of consumer behavior research, engineering constraint, and rapid iteration, and I thrived in that environment.
projects.involvement:
As one of the lead designers on Google's Mobile Search team, I owned interaction design across a range of high-visibility features — from local search and business discovery to query suggestions and contextual result formats. I worked directly with product managers, engineers, and user researchers to move from insight to shipped product at Google scale.

I was embedded in rapid iteration cycles, contributing to everything from early concept sketches and Figma flows to detailed interaction specs and QA reviews. I also contributed to internal design systems and component libraries that helped scale a consistent mobile search experience across teams.

Beyond the immediate work, I helped establish design patterns for touch-native mobile UI at a time when the discipline was genuinely being invented. The experiences I worked on reached hundreds of millions of users and shaped how people interact with Google on mobile to this day.

projects.title: Agentic OS
projects.description:
AgenticOS was an early experiment in AI-native productivity — a browser-based OS-like environment where professionals could build and run agentic, always-on applications without requiring full control of a physical machine. Built about a year before OpenClaw debuted, it served as a proving ground for what an AI-first OS could look like.

AI wasn't bolted on as isolated features — it was the foundation. Every layer of the experience was designed around intelligent automation, natural language interaction, and persistent agentic task execution.

Core explorations included a cross-app memory layer that made relevant knowledge instantly available to any application without requiring complex integrations, and a visual layer giving applications real-time awareness of on-screen content for true OS-wide multimodal capability.

Core Applications

Productivity Suite:

- **Notes** - Rich text editor with AI-powered RAG chat for intelligent note searching and content generation
- **Text Editor** - Full-featured document editing with syntax highlighting
- **Calculator** - Standard mathematical operations
- **Mail** - Email management with Resend integration
- **File Manager** - Complete file system navigation and management

Creative Tools:

- **Paint** - Canvas-based drawing application with Fabric.js
- **Photo Editor** - Advanced image editing with AI assistant for automated enhancements
- **Photo Viewer** - Image gallery and viewing capabilities
- **Music Player** - Audio playback with metadata support

Development & System:

- **Terminal** - Command-line interface for system operations
- **App Builder** - AI-powered application creation wizard
- **Agent Creator** - Build custom AI agents and workflows
- **System Preferences** - OS configuration and settings
- **Documentation** - Integrated help and API documentation

AI-Enhanced Apps:

- **Browser** - Web browsing with AI chat panel and agentic task execution (e.g., "find cheapest flights to NYC")
- **OSChat** - Universal AI assistant with voice command integration + agentic abilities (orchestration, service discovery)
- **Oracle** - Advanced AI consultation and analysis
- **Willbot Game** - Interactive AI character gaming experience

AI Features & Capabilities

Intelligent Command Layer:
- **Voice command** processing and natural language understanding
- **Agentic task** execution ("open browser and find me cheap flights")
- **Cross-app** intelligent routing and coordination

AI-Powered Content:

- **Notes** with RAG-based AI chat for content discovery
- **Photo editing** with AI enhancement suggestions
- **Browser** with specialized agents (flight search, general web tasks)
- **Real-time** AI assistance across applications via realtime vision

Modular AI Architecture:

- **Custom** agent creation and deployment
- **App-specific** AI command registration
- **Intelligent** workflow orchestration
- **Background** AI processing and sync

Voice & Natural Language:

- **Continuous voice** chat capabilities
- **Voice command** execution across all apps
- **Natural language** to system action translation
projects.involvement: Working alongside a confidential client, I conceived, designed, and built AgenticOS from the ground up — responsible for the full stack, from UX and interaction design to implementation in TypeScript and Next.js. I integrated Supabase and Postgres/PGVector for the persistent memory and RAG layer, OpenAI for NLU and agentic task execution, Hugging Face for model inference, and built the entire system using Cursor and Claude as core development tools.

essays.title: AI Governance for Product & Design folks
essays.content:
AI interfaces being rapidly adopted across industries only serves to highlight the need for thoughtful AI governance. (The use of a hyper-realistic AI avatar in a courtroom recently emphasized both the potential and the actual ethical complexities of AI across numerous contexts -- my previous post addressed this briefly).

By the book: AI Governance refers to the structured set of policies, frameworks, processes, and oversight mechanisms designed to ensure that AI systems are developed and used responsibly, ethically, and transparently. It encompasses addressing potential risks, safeguarding user rights, aligning AI behaviors with societal values, and ensuring accountability throughout the lifecycle of AI technologies.

Some practical guidelines for companies (and design/product teams) integrating AI into their product offerings include:

- Transparency: Clearly indicate when users are interacting with AI to build trust and prevent unintended manipulation. Let's trust, yet verify. And then verify again. (And again.)
- Diverse Expertise: Engage cross-functional teams -- including ethicists, psychologists, UX designers, and technologists -- to thoroughly understand and address ethical considerations. The concept of "UX" is only expanding discipline-wise.
- User Agency: Provide users with clear options to manage their interactions with AI, especially in emotionally or ethically sensitive scenarios. This might involve transferring to an actual human to complete a task, or reverting to a completely non-AI enabled experience.
- Continuous Evaluation: Regularly assess and refine AI experiences based on user feedback and evolving ethical standards to ensure ongoing alignment with human values. 

If you're new to AI governance (alongside most of the world), here's something of a kickstarter to enhance your own understanding, and to perhaps share around your organization a bit more broadly:

Starting Points:

Books:
- "AI Ethics: A Textbook" by Mark Coeckelbergh
- "Human Compatible: Artificial Intelligence and the Problem of Control" by Stuart Russell
- "Weapons of Math Destruction" by Cathy O'Neil
- "AI Fairness: Designing Equal Opportunity Algorithms" by Derek Leben

Online Resources:
- AI Ethics Guidelines by the European Commission
- AI Now Institute Reports

Intermediate Learning:

Courses:
- "Ethics of AI" by the University of Helsinki
- "AI for Everyone" by Andrew Ng on Coursera

Podcasts:
- "The AI Alignment Podcast" by Lucas Perry
- "AI Today Podcast" by Cognilytica

Advanced Exploration:

Research & Papers:
- "Artificial Intelligence and Life in 2030" (Stanford's One Hundred Year Study on Artificial Intelligence)

Events & Workshops:
- AI ethics and governance panels at conferences such as NeurIPS, AAAI, or SXSW
- Workshops by organizations like The Alan Turing Institute

Effective governance strategies not only safeguard user interests but also position businesses to responsibly harness AI’s transformative potential.

essays.title: AI/LLM on-device capability & information privacy
essays.content:
Working with on-device AI/ML models to preserve privacy (especially in the space of healthcare/therapy) is only getting more important... Now that we've moved very solidly into the era of AI-based therapists (or the very least, "sympathetic ears "-- https://lnkd.in/euTqBi82), it's more important than ever to be sure this data remains as private as possible. 

To bring it back to AI Governance: the ability to share that "AI on-phone functionality does not transmit patient information to outside (i.e. OpenAI) foundation models" is an important policy to stand behind.

With the news that Google is planning an on-device Gemma Nano implementation for iOS (already available for Android), folks (especially within healthcare/behavioral health) are thinking more than ever about the fact that, up until now, having LLM-like functionality on-device has been somewhat prohibitive without leveraging a foundation model like OpenAI, Anthropic, or Llama (each of which requires a network call to an API). 

Good news, though! I took the weekend to experiment with some of the already available on-device LLM, OCR, image recognition, and embedding creation models -- and came away encouraged to say the least. 

With the help of Cursor and XCode's terminal tools, as well as the excellent https://lnkd.in/ehGu9eha, I was able to get something up and running relatively quickly with the attached results. 

Very proof of concept-y but, again -- the future of advanced, on-device capabilities is bright.

On device models I used: Core ML LLM (Mistral 7B Int4), MobileBERT embeddings, sqlite-vec, Vision OCR, Local RAG libs (Swiftrag / LumoKit), Accelerate cosine sim blog.
 
From here, agentic implementations, visualizations, alerts based on smart devices (Oura ring), patient empowerment through data access... are all looking possible.

essays.title: AI Agent Accountability: Who’s Responsible When No One’s Home?
essays.content:
A few weeks ago, I received a reply to an email from from Vint Cerf — a colleague of mine from my time at Google, and an unimaginably kind human being. Kind enough to have responded to several other of my mostly inane messages… penned with an earnest, perhaps foolhardy sort of curiosity related to one topic or another about which it wouldn’t be a stretch to call him a prodigy. I calibrated my odds at an actual reply from him personally from somewhere in the low single digits, to, say a quadrillion or so. To my genuine astonishment, he wrote back. And we established what I like to think of as a friendly, if entirely infrequent, penpal-type of “acquaintanceship”.

I’d reached out to him about a paper he and Bob Kahn wrote in 1988 concerning “Knowbots” — a sort of proto-concept for AI-based agents that could roam networks, gather information, and act on behalf of users. The original paper is well worth the read, if for no other reason than to reinforce for all of us that while there are very smart people who walk among us all the time, there are very few genuine visionaries.

As for the title of his paper (co-published with Bob), if you substitute “Knowbot” for the contemporary concept of an autonomous AI agent, you’re basically up to speed. Prescient doesn’t begin to scratch the surface of the fact that he and Bob wrote this paper in 1988. Accurately predicting the rise of not only agents, but autonomous, always-on agents.

Vint’s reply to my rather innocuous email regarding his Knowbots paper — which he’d shared with me some time earlier — was generous by its very nature and (of course) keenly insightful & very sharp. In the course of his brief reply, he noted three things he and Bob hadn’t fully (entirely understandably) anticipated when they conceived of Knowbots (autonomous agents…in 1988): 1) agent accountability, 2) agent audit trails, and 3) agent registration. Nearly four decades later, those three gaps are still wide open — and as autonomous AI agents proliferate across enterprise, finance, healthcare, critical infrastructure, and even defense and military use cases, they’re becoming urgent.

Here’s the thing: as I noodle on these topics as they apply to the contemporary version of agents — I can’t help but think we may be applying the wrong (or at least, outdated) framework(s).

The Problem With “Accountability” as We Know It
When we talk about accountability in human systems — legal, financial, institutional — we’re really talking about a deterrence mechanism. You audit people in order to deter a certain type of behavior (i.e., cheating or evading) which works primarily because they know they’re being watched. Liability exists because consequences are felt (or at the very least, the threat of consequences). You require authorization because power without constraint is dangerous in the hands of a conscious actor who can choose to abuse it.

The thing is, and not to overstate the obvious, but AI agents aren’t conscious. They don’t fear consequence. They don’t have a sense of self-preservation that makes the threat of punishment meaningful. Applying a human accountability framework to a non-human system isn’t just a category error — it’s potentially a dangerous one. It creates the illusion of control without the substance of it.

So what do we actually need? I’d argue we need to decompose “accountability” into three distinct and addressable problems:

1. Identity — Who sent this agent?

2. Authorization — What is it permitted to do, and under whose authority?

3. Attribution — What did it actually do, and can that record be disputed?

These are not the same problem. Conflating them — as most current frameworks do — leads to solutions that are partial at best and misleading at worst.

The Authorization Problem Gets Thornier
Even if we solve identity and attribution cleanly, authorization raises questions that don’t have tidy answers. Whose authorization framework applies?

Consider an AI agent deployed by a U.S. financial firm, operating on infrastructure in Ireland, querying data held in Singapore, executing trades that affect a Japanese pension fund. Which jurisdiction’s rules govern what this agent is “permitted” to do? What happens when those rules conflict?

This isn’t hypothetical. It’s the current state of enterprise AI deployment. And the honest answer is: we don’t have a coherent cross-jurisdictional authorization framework for autonomous agents. We barely have one for humans.

What’s Already Being Built

To be fair, the infrastructure community isn’t standing still. Several promising approaches are emerging:

Decentralized Identifiers (DIDs) and Verifiable Credentials — Developed under W3C standards, DIDs allow agents to carry cryptographically verifiable identity that doesn’t depend on any centralized authority. Think of it as a passport that can’t be forged and doesn’t require a government to issue. Applied to agents, this means an agent can prove who deployed it, what version it is, and what it’s been authorized to do — without requiring a phone call back to a central server.

SPIFFE/SPIRE — A framework originally developed for microservices that assigns cryptographic identities to workloads. Being actively explored for AI agent deployments, particularly in enterprise environments where agents need to authenticate to internal systems without exposing credentials.

OpenID Connect for Agents (OIDC-A) — An emerging extension of the widely-used OIDC authentication standard, specifically designed to handle the delegation chains that appear when an agent acts on behalf of a user who acts on behalf of an organization. The critical innovation here is the ability to encode not just who the agent is, but the chain of authorization that led to its current permissions.

Verifiable Execution Logs — Blockchain-anchored or cryptographically signed logs that record what an agent did in a tamper-evident way. Unlike traditional audit logs (which can be modified by whoever controls the server), a verifiable execution log creates an immutable record that any party can independently verify.

A Proposal: The Cryptographic Accountability Stack
What I’d advocate for — and what several teams are quietly building toward — is a layered cryptographic accountability stack for AI agents:

Layer 1 — Identity: Every agent carries a DID-based identity credential, cryptographically signed by its deploying organization. This credential includes version information, training lineage, and a policy hash describing what the agent is authorized to do.

Layer 2 — Authorization: Permissions are encoded as signed, time-bounded tokens using an OIDC-A-style delegation chain. An agent can only act within the scope of its current token. When scope expands, a new authorization event is logged and signed.

Layer 3 — Execution: Every significant action the agent takes is logged to a verifiable execution record — cryptographically chained so that any modification is detectable. This log is the audit trail, not a server-side database that can be quietly edited.

Layer 4 — Dispute Resolution: Because the logs are verifiable by third parties, disputes about what an agent did — and whether it was authorized to do so — can be resolved without relying on the word of the party being accused.

This isn’t a theoretical architecture. The components exist. What’s missing is standardization, adoption incentives, and frankly, the urgency that tends to follow a high-profile failure.

The Harder Question

I want to close with the thing that bothers me most about how this conversation is unfolding in policy circles and enterprise boardrooms.

Accountability frameworks have historically been applied to entities that couldn’t fully advocate for themselves — and those frameworks have often said more about the needs of the powerful than the interests of the accountable. I’m not drawing a direct equivalence here. I am saying that when we design control frameworks for non-human intelligence, we should be rigorous about what we’re actually solving for: Is this about establishing genuine oversight? Or is it about creating the appearance of oversight while insulating decision-makers from consequences?

The cryptographic stack I’ve described above is genuinely useful. But it only works if the humans deploying these agents are honest about what they’re authorizing. A signed permission token for “manage client portfolios” that quietly encompasses “execute trades without human review” isn’t accountability — it’s laundered liability.

Vint Cerf and Bob Kahn didn’t anticipate the accountability problem in 1988 because the stakes were low (relatively) and the agents were simple conceptually. The stakes aren’t low anymore. And the agents are getting less simple by the week.

We should build the infrastructure that matches the moment — not borrow frameworks designed for a world where accountability required a (human’s notion of) conscience.
